title: Serial Neurologic Checks: Trends Beat Snapshots
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: A neurologic check is valuable because of change over time. New decline in consciousness, pupils, speech, strength, coordination, behavior, or headache pattern requires prompt escalation rather than waiting for the next routine interval.
recognize: Subtle slowing, new confusion, unequal pupils, drift, new weakness, worsening headache, vomiting, or seizure activity can precede major deterioration.
Sedatives, hypoglycemia, hypoxia, infection, and metabolic disturbances can mimic or worsen neurologic decline and must be considered.
priorities: Compare findings with the documented baseline and prior examination.
Escalate acute change immediately and support ABCs while further evaluation is arranged.
assessMonitor: Trend level of consciousness, orientation, pupils, speech, facial symmetry, limb strength, sensation when indicated, vital signs, oxygenation, glucose when relevant, and headache/vomiting.
interventions: Maintain safety, apply ordered monitoring, position appropriately for the condition, and communicate the exact change and time last known at baseline.
medicationSafety: Review sedatives, opioids, anticoagulants, insulin, and other agents that can alter mentation or bleeding risk.
teaching: Families should report sudden behavior, speech, movement, or responsiveness changes rather than assuming the patient is sleeping.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated where permitted, but interpretation of neurologic change and escalation remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Documenting a lower score as a routine variation without comparing it with the previous neurologic baseline.
oneLinePearl: Neuro checks are about change—small trends can signal big trouble.
sourceBasis: AHA/ASA 2026 acute ischemic stroke guideline nursing resources

title: Post-Stroke Dysphagia: Screen Before Swallowing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After acute stroke, swallowing impairment can be silent. Oral food, fluids, and medications should follow the institution's dysphagia-screening pathway; coughing is not required for aspiration to occur.
recognize: Wet voice, drooling, pocketing, coughing, throat clearing, prolonged meals, desaturation, or recurrent fever can suggest dysphagia/aspiration.
A patient may aspirate without obvious coughing.
priorities: Keep oral intake on hold until the required swallow screen/assessment is completed when indicated.
Escalate respiratory distress, repeated aspiration signs, or inability to manage secretions.
assessMonitor: Monitor voice quality, oral motor control, secretion management, lung sounds, oxygenation, temperature, hydration, and nutritional intake.
interventions: Follow prescribed texture/liquid recommendations, positioning, pacing, oral-care, and medication-administration modifications.
medicationSafety: Do not crush medications unless formulation safety has been verified; enteric-coated or extended-release products may be unsafe to alter.
teaching: Use only the prescribed food/liquid consistency and swallowing strategies until reassessed.
delegationScope: Meal assistance may be delegated only when the plan is stable and clear; new swallowing difficulty requires licensed reassessment/escalation.
examTrap: Giving water to 'test' swallowing before the formal screening pathway is completed.
oneLinePearl: No cough does not mean no aspiration.
sourceBasis: AHA/ASA 2026 acute ischemic stroke guideline nursing guidance

title: External Ventricular Drain Safety: Level, Clamp, Escalate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: EVD drainage depends on an exact reference level and prescribed system height. Unplanned position changes, disconnection, sudden drainage change, or neurologic deterioration require immediate action according to neurocritical-care protocol.
recognize: Overdrainage can occur if the collection system is too low; underdrainage can occur if it is too high or obstructed.
Cloudy CSF, fever, drainage-system breach, headache, vomiting, or declining consciousness may signal complication.
priorities: Maintain the prescribed reference level and clamp/level before repositioning according to local protocol.
Escalate abrupt neurologic decline, disconnection, absent drainage with deterioration, or unexpectedly large drainage.
assessMonitor: Trend neuro status, ICP when displayed, CSF volume/color, dressing/system integrity, temperature, and headache/vomiting.
interventions: Keep the closed system intact, use sterile technique for any authorized handling, and follow explicit clamp/transport/re-leveling policy.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulant/antiplatelet exposure and sedatives can materially change bleeding or assessment risk and should be reconciled.
teaching: Patients/families should not adjust the drainage system or bed height without staff assistance.
delegationScope: EVD management is highly policy- and competency-dependent; PN/LVN role is monitoring and immediate escalation unless specifically authorized.
examTrap: Repositioning the patient without re-leveling or following the ordered clamp protocol.
oneLinePearl: With an EVD, a few centimeters can change drainage dramatically.
sourceBasis: AHA/ASA 2022 spontaneous ICH guideline neurocritical-care principles

title: Seizure Precautions: Protect First, Observe Precisely
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: During a seizure, protect the patient from injury, maintain airway safety, time the event, and observe features that help classify it. Do not restrain forcefully and do not place objects in the mouth.
recognize: Aura, gaze deviation, focal jerking, automatisms, loss of awareness, generalized stiffening/jerking, cyanosis, incontinence, and postictal confusion are useful observations.
Repeated seizures without recovery, prolonged convulsive activity, injury, pregnancy, hypoglycemia, or respiratory compromise raise urgency.
priorities: Protect the head, remove hazards, position for airway drainage when feasible, time the event, and summon help according to the seizure action plan.
Afterward, assess breathing, circulation, neurologic recovery, glucose when indicated, and injuries.
assessMonitor: Record onset, duration, body parts involved, eye/head position, responsiveness, breathing/color, incontinence, postictal state, and potential triggers.
interventions: Maintain side-lying recovery positioning when appropriate, suction/oxygen per need and order, and preserve privacy.
medicationSafety: Rescue benzodiazepines and other emergency medications require exact product, route, timing, and respiratory monitoring according to the action plan.
redFlags: Ongoing convulsion beyond the patient's emergency threshold
teaching: Do not put anything in the mouth; follow the individualized rescue-medication and EMS plan.
delegationScope: Observation/support may be shared with trained staff, but rescue medication, neurologic assessment, and escalation must follow law/policy/competency.
examTrap: Forcing a tongue blade into the mouth to prevent tongue biting.
oneLinePearl: Protect, time, observe, recover—never restrain or put objects in the mouth.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. seizure first-aid and emergency neurologic practice principles

title: Lumbar Puncture Aftercare: Watch the Patient, Not a Bed-Rest Myth
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: After lumbar puncture, monitor neurologic status, puncture site, headache pattern, hydration, and ordered activity. Prolonged flat bed rest is not a universal requirement and should not replace assessment of a severe or atypical post-procedure headache.
recognize: Post-dural puncture headache is typically positional, but fever, focal deficit, altered consciousness, severe persistent back pain, or progressive weakness requires urgent evaluation.
Bleeding risk is higher with coagulopathy or antithrombotic exposure.
priorities: Follow the ordered post-procedure positioning/activity plan.
Escalate severe nonpostural headache, neurologic deficit, fever, CSF leak, or significant bleeding.
assessMonitor: Monitor vital signs, neuro status, puncture site, headache characteristics, hydration, and mobility tolerance.
interventions: Provide ordered analgesia/fluids and protect the puncture site.
medicationSafety: Reconcile anticoagulants/antiplatelets and sedatives around the procedure according to prescriber/protocol.
teaching: Report severe or worsening headache, fever, drainage, weakness, or numbness after discharge.
delegationScope: Routine vitals and comfort measures may be delegated with parameters; neurologic change requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every severe headache after LP is benign and treating only with bed rest.
oneLinePearl: After LP, pattern matters—positional headache is common, neurologic change is not.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. procedural neurology practice principles

title: After Craniotomy: Small Changes Can Signal Big Problems
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Post-craniotomy deterioration may reflect bleeding, edema, seizure, hydrocephalus, infection, or medication effect. New neurologic change, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, or wound/CSF drainage requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Increasing somnolence, focal weakness, aphasia, pupil change, severe headache, vomiting, or new seizure are concerning.
Clear drainage from the wound/nose/ear, fever, or wound erythema can signal CSF leak or infection depending on surgery.
priorities: Compare with the immediate postoperative neuro baseline and escalate acute change.
Protect airway, maintain ordered head/neck positioning, and avoid activities that increase pressure when contraindicated.
assessMonitor: Trend neuro status, pupils, strength, vital signs, pain, nausea/vomiting, incision/drainage, seizure activity, and intake/output.
interventions: Maintain prescribed positioning, seizure/fall precautions, and wound/drain care; coordinate urgent imaging/evaluation when ordered.
medicationSafety: Opioids/sedatives can obscure neuro decline; antiepileptic and steroid plans vary by procedure and should be followed exactly.
teaching: Report new severe headache, weakness, seizure, fever, or clear wound/nasal drainage immediately.
delegationScope: Post-craniotomy neurologic interpretation and acute deterioration are licensed-nurse/RN/provider responsibilities.
examTrap: Explaining new somnolence as expected anesthesia effect without comparing the neurologic baseline.
oneLinePearl: After brain surgery, never normalize a new neurologic deficit.

title: Suspected Spinal Cord Injury: Protect Alignment and Breathing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: With suspected unstable spinal injury, airway/breathing and spinal alignment are simultaneous priorities. New weakness, sensory loss, hypotension with bradycardia, or worsening respiratory effort requires emergency escalation.
recognize: High cervical injury can impair ventilation; neurogenic shock may produce hypotension with relative bradycardia and warm skin.
Spinal shock and neurologic level cannot be safely inferred from one early assessment.
priorities: Maintain ordered spinal motion restriction and use trained team movement techniques.
Escalate respiratory decline, progressive weakness, new bowel/bladder dysfunction, or hemodynamic instability.
assessMonitor: Trend breathing, oxygenation, strength/sensation, pain, BP/HR, skin temperature/perfusion, bladder distention, and level-specific deficits.
interventions: Support airway, pressure-area protection, neutral alignment, log-roll/team turns when ordered, and DVT/skin prevention plan.
medicationSafety: Sedatives/opioids can worsen respiratory compromise or obscure neurologic change; vasoactive therapy requires monitored settings and scope verification.
complications: Autonomic dysreflexia later in susceptible injuries
teaching: Do not twist or sit up independently until the injury/stability plan allows it.
delegationScope: Transfers/turns require trained personnel and a clear plan; unstable neurologic or hemodynamic changes require licensed assessment.
examTrap: Prioritizing a detailed motor exam over an unstable airway in a high cervical injury.
oneLinePearl: Protect the cord without losing the airway.
sourceBasis: Contemporary U.S. spinal-cord injury emergency care principles

title: Autonomic Dysreflexia: Sit Up, Search, Escalate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: In a susceptible spinal-cord injury, sudden severe hypertension with headache, flushing/sweating above the lesion, bradycardia or other autonomic symptoms is an emergency. Sit the patient upright when appropriate, loosen restrictive items, rapidly search for common triggers—especially bladder problems—and escalate.
recognize: Bladder distention/blocked catheter is a common trigger; bowel impaction, skin pressure, tight clothing, wounds, and procedures are others.
Symptoms can be dramatic even when the trigger seems minor.
priorities: Raise the head/assist upright, loosen constrictive clothing, check urinary drainage first, and obtain frequent BP while escalating according to protocol.
Remove the trigger safely and administer ordered antihypertensive therapy if needed.
assessMonitor: Trend BP/HR, headache, flushing/sweating, catheter patency, bowel/skin triggers, and neurologic symptoms.
interventions: Correct obvious noxious stimuli within scope and maintain close reassessment until BP and symptoms normalize.
medicationSafety: Rapid-acting antihypertensive choice depends on protocol; avoid unsupervised long-acting therapy that can cause prolonged hypotension after trigger removal.
teaching: Know personal triggers and emergency steps; keep bladder/bowel equipment and action-plan information available.
delegationScope: Trigger checks may be shared with trained staff, but the emergency requires immediate licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Laying the patient flat because the blood pressure is high.
oneLinePearl: Autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, check the bladder, remove the trigger, escalate.
sourceBasis: Contemporary U.S. spinal-cord injury emergency care principles

title: Neurogenic Bladder and Bowel: Prevent Retention, Infection, and Skin Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Neurogenic bladder/bowel care is a scheduled prevention strategy, not just symptom treatment. Retention, high-pressure bladder, constipation/impaction, infection, autonomic dysreflexia, and skin injury are preventable complications when the individualized program is followed consistently.
recognize: Overflow leakage can coexist with retention; cloudy urine alone does not diagnose UTI.
Constipation or impaction can worsen bladder function and trigger autonomic dysreflexia in susceptible patients.
priorities: Follow the prescribed catheterization/voiding and bowel schedule.
Escalate fever/systemic symptoms, new retention, autonomic dysreflexia, hematuria, or severe abdominal distention.
assessMonitor: Monitor output, bladder fullness, continence pattern, urine symptoms, bowel frequency/consistency, abdominal distention, skin integrity, and hydration plan.
interventions: Use clean/sterile catheter technique as prescribed, skin protection, bowel regimen, positioning, hydration, and mobility plan.
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, alpha blockers, laxatives, suppositories, and antibiotics should be used for their actual indication; avoid reflex antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria unless specifically indicated.
teaching: Consistency with the bladder/bowel program prevents emergencies better than waiting for symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine program steps may be delegated only to trained staff according to policy; new retention, infection, bleeding, or AD requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Treating every cloudy urine episode with antibiotics without symptoms or culture-based indication.
oneLinePearl: Neurogenic elimination care works best on schedule, not in crisis.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. neurogenic bladder/bowel rehabilitation principles

title: Acute Intracerebral Hemorrhage Monitoring: Smooth, Stable, Escalate
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acute ICH requires close neurologic and hemodynamic surveillance because expansion and secondary injury can occur early. Smooth BP control, anticoagulant-reversal awareness, seizure recognition, airway protection, and rapid escalation of decline are central nursing priorities.
recognize: Worsening headache, vomiting, declining consciousness, new focal deficit, seizure, or pupil change may reflect hematoma expansion, hydrocephalus, edema, or herniation.
Anticoagulant use materially changes emergency management.
priorities: Escalate any neurologic decline immediately.
Support ordered smooth BP management and verify anticoagulant/antiplatelet history promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend neuro exam, pupils, BP variability, oxygenation, glucose, temperature, seizure activity, and signs of raised ICP.
interventions: Maintain airway safety, prescribed head positioning, seizure precautions, and monitored medication delivery.
medicationSafety: Current AHA/ASA guidance emphasizes targeted reversal for anticoagulant-associated ICH and does not support routine prophylactic antiseizure medication in the absence of seizures; medication decisions remain provider-driven.
teaching: Recovery planning begins early, but acute neurologic worsening always takes priority over routine rehabilitation tasks.
delegationScope: Frequent acute ICH monitoring and interpretation require licensed nurse/RN-level oversight; PN/LVN role depends on setting and policy.
examTrap: Assuming prophylactic seizure medication is automatically required for every ICH patient.
oneLinePearl: In ICH, prevent secondary injury and act on change immediately.
sourceBasis: AHA/ASA 2022 Guideline for Management of Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage
